On the 4th day of hospital admission due to pneumonia, a 69-year-old woman develops non-bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. She is currently treated with ceftriaxone. Despite the resolution of fever after the first 2 days of admission, her temperature is now 38.5°C (101.3°F). On physical examination, she has mild generalized abdominal tenderness without abdominal guarding or rebound tenderness. Laboratory studies show re-elevation of leukocyte counts. Ceftriaxone is discontinued. Given the most likely diagnosis in this patient, which of the following is the most sensitive test?
 ?

                    ### Question
                    On the 4th day of hospital admission due to pneumonia, a 69-year-old woman develops non-bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. She is currently treated with ceftriaxone. Despite the resolution of fever after the first 2 days of admission, her temperature is now 38.5°C (101.3°F). On physical examination, she has mild generalized abdominal tenderness without abdominal guarding or rebound tenderness. Laboratory studies show re-elevation of leukocyte counts. ### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient, treated with ceftriaxone for pneumonia, develops non-bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever, with re-elevation of leukocyte counts on the 4th day of hospital admission. These symptoms are highly suggestive of Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI), a common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea. The most sensitive test for diagnosing CDI is the nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), which detects the presence of C. difficile toxin genes with high sensitivity. This aligns with standard medical consensus, as NAAT is preferred for its ability to accurately identify the presence of the pathogen's genetic material, even in the absence of active toxin production. Other options, such as enzyme immunoassay for glutamate dehydrogenase or stool culture, are less sensitive and may not detect all cases of CDI. The retrieved evidence paths support the link between antibiotic use, diarrhea, and C. difficile infection, reinforcing the appropriateness of NAAT as the most sensitive diagnostic test in this clinical scenario.
